newsitem.title: USA: CompuServe faces shareholders on Friday.
newsitem.headline: CompuServe faces shareholders on Friday.

text.p: CompuServe Corp, which has been losing money, subscribers and executives lately, could face some hard questions at its shareholder meeting Friday.

The Columbus, Ohio-based online provider on February 20 reported its third-quarter loss narrowed from the second quarter. But days before the report, President and Chief Executive Officer Robert Massey resigned.
The president of its international operations and its chief technical officer also departed in the past year, and its third-quarter report noted a decline in subscribers.
While analysts believe CompuServe can return to profitability, they said it must put someone at the helm very soon and then clarify its strategy.
"The major questions they need to address are, one, who's going to lead the company, and two, what is the company?" said Nesbitt Burns Securities Inc analyst Abhishek Gami.
CompuServe is the second-largest online provider, with about five million subscribers including a licensee in Japan. America Online Inc is larger with about eight million.

CompuServe has said its focus is the business market rather than the mass consumer audience. But it is unclear how it will differentiate itself from competitors or how profitable that market can be, Gami said.

A spokeswoman said Chairman Frank Salizzoni, who is acting chief executive officer, was not available for an interview. He is also president of CompuServe parent H&R Block Inc, the tax-preparation company, which owns 80 percent of CompuServe.
Last year, CompuServe exited a short-lived consumer online service for novices called WOW!. Its flagship subscriber service appeals mainly to business-oriented professionals.

Its Network Services provides online services for large corporations such as Visa International, for whom it processes more than one billion authorizations a year. CompuServe also plans to launch new products for small businesses.
Salomon Bros Inc analyst Marc Usem said the corporate business has been doing quite well and the plan to offer value-added services for small business was viable.
Still, Usem agreed that CompuServe must "solidify its vision" and replace Massey "sooner rather than later. They need somebody in that seat to help guide the company forward."
Usem rated CompuServe shares as a buy. "I think it's a value play. I think there is considerable value in the Network Services asset" alone, as well as potential elsewhere, he said.

Goldman Sachs also recommended the stock, which has been mired at about $10 on the Nasdaq. It was priced at $30 in April 1996 when Block offered 20 percent of CompuServe in an initial public offering.

The shareholder meeting, scheduled at 0900 EST (1400 GMT) at the company's suburban Columbus headquarters, may be the first of two this year. This week's meeting is actually the one slated to report to shareholders on the year ended in April 1995. A spokeswoman said another shareholder meeting may be in the fall.
